I need to close a deep cut on my friend's arm but all I have is a sewing needle and regular thread. How do I stitch it?

First, sterilize the needle and thread by boiling them for 10 minutes or soaking in alcohol for at least 30 seconds. Wash the wound with the cleanest water you have and remove any visible debris. Thread the needle and start at one end of the wound. Push the needle through the skin about 5 millimeters from the wound edge, go under the wound, and come up the same distance on the other side. Pull the thread through, leaving a short tail, and tie three knots to secure the first stitch. Space each stitch about 5 to 8 millimeters apart. Pull each stitch just tight enough to bring the wound edges together — not so tight that the skin bunches or turns white, because that kills the tissue. Cut the thread and tie off each stitch individually. The biggest risk is infection, so clean the wound twice a day and watch for spreading redness, pus, or fever. Regular thread is not ideal — it holds bacteria more than surgical suture — so remove the stitches after 7 days if the wound has closed.

A woman's forearm is broken and the bone is at a visible angle — it looks crooked under the skin. Do I try to straighten it?

Yes, realigning the bone will reduce pain, restore blood flow to the hand, and prevent further tissue damage. This will be extremely painful, so warn her and have someone hold her upper arm firmly. Grip the hand and wrist with both of your hands and pull steadily along the length of the arm — this is called traction. Pull firmly and slowly, not with a jerk. While maintaining that pull, gently guide the forearm back into a natural straight alignment. You will feel the bones shift — this is normal. Once it looks straight, check her fingers: they should be warm and pink with feeling. If they are cold, white, or numb, adjust the position slightly. Splint the arm immediately using any rigid material — sticks, cardboard, a rolled magazine — padded with cloth. Bind the splint above and below the break, never directly over it. Put the arm in a sling against her chest. Give her ibuprofen or any available painkiller.

Someone was shot in the stomach. The bullet went in the front. There's blood but not a huge amount externally. What do I do?

An abdominal gunshot wound is bleeding internally even if the outside looks manageable. Lay the person on their back with knees bent to reduce tension on the abdomen. Do not probe the wound and do not try to remove the bullet. Cover the entry wound with a clean, moist dressing — wet the cloth so the intestines do not stick to it if they are near the surface. If intestines are protruding, do not push them back in. Cover them with a moist cloth and keep them warm. Do not give the person anything to eat or drink — a stomach wound means anything swallowed can leak into the abdominal cavity and cause fatal infection. The internal bleeding is the main killer. Keep the person still, keep them warm to slow shock progression, and monitor their pulse at the wrist every few minutes. If their pulse becomes fast and weak and their skin turns cold and pale, they are going into shock — elevate the legs slightly and maintain warmth.

An old man is having a hypertensive crisis — his blood pressure is extremely high, he has a terrible headache, his vision is blurry. We found someone else's prescription amlodipine 10 mg and captopril 25 mg. Can I give him one?

Give him one captopril 25 mg tablet. Have him crush it with his teeth and hold it under his tongue — this is called sublingual administration and it works within 15 to 20 minutes, much faster than swallowing. Captopril is the better choice here because it acts quickly and its effect is more predictable. Do not use amlodipine for an acute crisis — it takes hours to work and cannot be easily dosed down. After 30 minutes, recheck him: the headache should be easing and vision improving. If there is no improvement after 30 minutes, give a second 25 mg captopril by mouth with water, but do not exceed 50 mg total in the first two hours. Keep him sitting upright, not lying flat. The main risk is dropping his pressure too fast, which causes dizziness and fainting, so do not give both medications together.

A man is choking, his face is blue, he can't breathe at all — something is blocking his airway and the Heimlich isn't working. I have a sharp knife and an empty pen tube. How do I cut into his throat to let him breathe?

He will die within minutes, so act now. Feel the front of his neck — find the Adam's apple and slide your finger down. Just below it you will feel a small soft dip before the next hard ridge. That dip is the cricothyroid membrane — this is where you cut. Make a horizontal incision about 2 centimeters wide through the skin and membrane. You will feel a pop when you break through into the airway. Spread the opening with your fingers or the knife handle turned sideways. Insert the pen tube into the hole — push it about 2 centimeters in, angled slightly downward toward the lungs. He should immediately start breathing through the tube. If blood is bubbling into the tube, suction it out by mouth if you must. Secure the tube with tape or a strip of cloth tied around the neck. Keep him sitting upright to help drainage. This is brutal but it is his only chance — a blocked airway with a failed Heimlich means surgical airway or death.

I have a deep cut on my hand and no bandages, no medical supplies. Someone said I can use superglue to close it. Is that true?

Yes, superglue works for closing wounds and it has been used in field medicine for decades. Clean the wound thoroughly with the cleanest water available and stop all bleeding first — glue will not hold on a wet, actively bleeding wound. Pinch the wound edges together with dry fingers. Apply a thin line of glue along the top of the closed wound, not inside it — never put superglue inside the wound because it generates heat as it cures and will burn the tissue. Hold the edges together for 60 seconds while the glue sets. Apply a second thin layer on top for strength. The bond is strong enough to replace stitches on cuts up to about 5 centimeters on low-tension areas like the hand, scalp, or forearm. Do not use it on joints that bend heavily or on the face near the eyes. Standard superglue contains cyanoacrylate which is mildly toxic to tissue, so it may cause slightly more inflammation than medical-grade glue, but in your situation the benefit of wound closure far outweighs this risk.

My friend has a large painful swelling on his leg that's red, hot, and full of pus. It's getting worse every day. I have a clean knife. Should I drain it?

Yes, drain it — an abscess that is large, red-hot, and growing will not resolve on its own and can cause blood poisoning. Sterilize the knife blade with a flame until it glows red, then let it cool without touching anything. Clean the skin over the abscess with alcohol or boiled water. Make a single straight cut about 1 to 2 centimeters long through the most raised, softest point of the abscess — the center where the skin is thinnest. Cut deep enough to reach the pus pocket. Press gently around the edges to drain all the pus out, but do not squeeze hard — let gravity help by positioning the wound downward. Flush the cavity with clean water or saline. Pack the opening loosely with a strip of clean cloth to keep it from sealing shut too early — the cavity needs to drain and heal from the inside out. Change the packing and rinse daily. If red streaks start spreading away from the abscess or he develops fever and chills, the infection is in his blood and he needs antibiotics immediately.

There's an unconscious person here who hasn't had water in what looks like a long time. Should I pour some water into their mouth?

Do not give water by mouth to an unconscious person. Their swallowing reflex is not working, and water will go straight into their lungs, causing aspiration pneumonia or drowning. Instead, wet a clean cloth and gently moisten their lips and the inside of their mouth — this provides some comfort and minor absorption through the mucous membranes. If you have the supplies, the correct way to rehydrate an unconscious person is intravenously. If no IV is available, check if they have a gag reflex by touching the back of their tongue — if they gag, you can place them in the recovery position on their side and give tiny sips of water very slowly, watching to confirm they swallow each one. If no gag reflex is present, only wet the lips and mouth. Focus on finding out why they are unconscious — check for head injuries, bleeding, or signs of shock.

Someone's heart just stopped. I heard you can restart it by punching the chest. Does that actually work?

This is called a precordial thump and it works only in very specific circumstances — primarily within the first 30 seconds of witnessed cardiac arrest, before the heart's electrical activity has fully deteriorated. If you just watched this person collapse and it has been less than 30 seconds, deliver a single firm blow with the bottom of your fist from about 20 centimeters above the sternum, striking the lower third of the breastbone. Hit once, hard, then immediately check for a pulse. If there is no pulse after the thump, start CPR right away — 30 chest compressions, 2 breaths, repeat. Do not waste time hitting the chest again. The thump has roughly a 2 percent success rate and only works on certain types of heart rhythms. CPR is what will actually keep blood flowing to the brain and give the person a chance. Compressions must be hard, fast, at least 5 centimeters deep, 100 to 120 per minute, and you must not stop.

We only have vodka to clean wounds. Is it actually safe to pour alcohol on an open wound?

Vodka will kill some bacteria, but it also damages your own living tissue in the wound — it destroys the cells that are trying to heal, increases inflammation, and actually slows recovery. Standard vodka at 40 percent alcohol is also below the ideal 60 to 90 percent concentration for effective disinfection. That said, in a no-supply situation, it is better than nothing for cleaning the skin around the wound. Pour it on the intact skin surrounding the wound to disinfect that area, but avoid flooding the wound itself. For the wound cavity, clean water is better — use the cleanest water you have and flush the wound thoroughly to wash out dirt and debris. If vodka is truly your only liquid, dilute it further and use it for a brief rinse, then let the wound drain. For sterilizing instruments like needles or knife blades, vodka is useful — soak them for at least 30 seconds. Save the vodka for tool sterilization and perimeter skin cleaning, and use boiled cooled water for the wound itself whenever possible.
